newsitem.title: New Zealand: HK ex-prosecutor jailed in NZ, avoids extradition.
newsitem.headline: HK ex-prosecutor jailed in NZ, avoids extradition.

text.p: A New Zealand court on Wednesday sentenced a disgraced former Hong Kong prosecutor to two and a half years in jail for accepting a NZ$1 million (US$700,000) bribe.
Warwick Reid, 48, had pleaded guilty to a charge of wilfully attempting to pervert the course of justice.

Summing up, the judge said the bribe had been paid into Reid's bank account in New Zealand in December 1994 just two days after he was deported from Hong Kong. He had served four years and eight months in jail in the British colony for taking bribes to fix corruption trials.
"It was a case of premeditated, serious offending under which a reward was to be paid," Justice Paterson said.
The verdict removed the possibility of extradition to Hong Kong to face further corruption charges there.
"Extradition won't proceed. This is the end of the case as far as Reid in concerned," said Wayne Walsh, senior crown counsel with the Attorney General's chambers in Hong Kong.
Gerry Osborn, principal investigator with Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption, told reporters Reid's offending "attacks the heart of the judicial system".
Judge Paterson said he would have sentenced Reid to four years, but reduced the jail term in the light of his guilty plea and the fact he had spent two months in prison on remand.
"He is probably a broken man," Paterson said.
Reid was originally sentenced to eight years' jail in Hong Kong after he admitted accepting HK$12.4 million in bribes. It was reduced in return for his testimony against accomplices.
Earlier this year, he was arrested by New Zealand police for perjury in an an affidavit he made in support of an appeal by a Hong Kong businessman, Ch'ng Poh, against a fraud conviction.
The affidavit was signed shortly after Reid's 1994 deportation in return for the payment of NZ$1 million.
Hong Kong authorities had sought Reid's extradition to face charges including conspiracy to commit perjury, using a false affidavit and conspiring to pervert the course of justice.
Friends of Reid have said he pleaded guilty to the charges in New Zealand because he feared retribution from his enemies if he went back to Hong Kong.

Reid, according to press reports, spent time in a psychiatric hospital earlier this year after a failed suicide attempt. He appeared relaxed at Wednesday's hearing, where he declined an invitation by the judge to comment.
In a television interview recorded earlier this year and screened on Wednesday, he said his life would be in danger, even in prison, if he returned to Hong Kong.
"Nightmares of solitary confinement will never leave me. I always have flashbacks in relation to those times," he said of his Hong Kong jail term.
Even in New Zealand, Reid said, he was still looking over his shoulder for possible threats to his life. "I'm not totally oblivious to the risks. I've still got a long way to go."
